extracted.intended_audience: early-career biomedical researchers / junior faculty interested in NIH study section service
extracted.subtask_short: participating as NIH early career reviewer
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal policy summary about NIH's Early Career Reviewer pilot: who is targeted, how they are to be assigned, what their duties and limits are, and how to get nominated. Focused on junior investigators seeking review experience on NIH study sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer eligibility / target population
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH will take 'complete novice reviewers' — people who have not reviewed for NIH before, very early in their career, probably new investigators; SROs will be encouraged to seek out reviewers who have not yet received NIH funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page emphasizes targeting new investigators and those who have not previously served on NIH study sections; some anecdotes indicate that having an R01 is not a strict requirement and that the program is intended to help those early in their careers (e.g., K-awardees or unsuccessful but competitive applicants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Host institution and diversity prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority appears to be given to individuals who work at universities without copious amounts of NIH funding and to individuals who are underrepresented in science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes an effort to prioritize less-represented institutions and underrepresented groups, but also cautions that the program may be extended to many applicants 'out of a sense of fairness'—so selection may vary by SRO. Commentary includes both encouragement of diversity and skepticism that the program will remain exclusive to those priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment load limits and role restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Career Reviewers are to be invited for a one- or two-ad-hoc type stint with a review load of no more than two grants; they may not be primary assignments and may serve as tertiary/tertiary/4th reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post reports that SROs are encouraged to limit the load (no more than two grants) and to invite no more than one ECR per section meeting. There is mention that making them non-primary reviewers may be driven by legal/ federal advisory constraints; anecdotal reports, however, show some ECRs being allowed to select 4 grants and write full critiques and serve as a fourth reviewer—practices vary by panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO encouragement and meeting-level limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific Review Officers (SROs) are encouraged to include junior scientists and to invite an Early Career Reviewer to most meetings, but to limit to no more than one ECR per section meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post suggests SROs should view ECRs as reviewers-in-training; ECR visits may be 'off the books' for SRO metrics. This is practical guidance for how SROs should manage inclusion while balancing panel diversity and workload metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational participation mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: ECRs may be given access to the list of grants, asked to select grants to review, provide full written critiques (uploaded to eRA Commons), be granted IAR permission, and be allowed into the review/discussion phase; NIH-arranged travel may be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter’s anecdote describes being sent a list of grants, selecting four to critique, uploading critiques to Commons, receiving IAR permission, being considered a fourth reviewer in the meeting, and participating in discussions. This demonstrates variance in practice and what an ECR can expect in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to be nominated / application tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Junior faculty should get their CV in front of SROs for relevant study sections, cold-email SROs, ask associate-professor peers to forward CVs, or have Program Officers put in a good word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips: make it easy for busy SROs (concise CVs), ask colleagues who are on panels to recommend you, mention the NIH podcast comment if desired. Experienced investigators are encouraged to forward names; self-nomination by emailing that you 'heard a rumor' is presented as acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended benefits / learning outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Serving as an ECR is intended to teach junior scientists how the NIH grant review process really works, improve their grantsmanship, strategic thinking about careers, and produce a more sanguine response to receiving reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author and commenters emphasize educational value: learning how to write grants, seeing fair/civil/critical discussions, and gaining perspective that can improve applicants' own proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and potential tokenism (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a risk that ECR participation becomes token (tertiary/4th reviewer whose input 'doesn't matter') or an unnecessary expense if the visit yields little meaningful contribution; entrenched review culture can still marginalize new voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several comments warn that ECRs might be treated as 'training' observers whose contributions do not influence outcomes, and that panels may remain conservative and biased toward established investigators. The author suggests NIH should instead invite more young investigators as full contributing members rather than token trainees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal / procedural constraints affecting role
rubrics_metrics.description: Some aspects of the ECR visits (e.g., non-reviewing visits or limiting assignment types) may be influenced by authorizing legislation or Federal advisory rules, constraining how ECRs can be assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes a rumor that making ECRs non-reviewing visitors might be 'illegal under authorizing legislation or Federal advisory rules,' which may explain why SROs plan minimal loads and non-primary roles; this explains variability and caution among SROs.
